decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: Which lane should you normally drive in, and when may you leave it?
cards.back: Drive in the right-hand lane unless you are passing, or stopped vehicles, a crash or another obstacle forces you over the center line, in which case yield to oncoming traffic first.

cards.front: On which roads and with which signs may you also leave the right lane?
cards.back: Leaving the right lane is also allowed on roads with three or more marked lanes, on one-way streets with two or more lanes, and when signs or signals on a two-way multi-lane highway direct you left.

cards.front: When may you cross the center line to turn?
cards.back: You may cross the center line to turn left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway.

cards.front: When may you leave the right lane for emergencies or construction?
cards.back: You may leave the right lane to go around a stopped emergency vehicle once it is safe, or when road construction is near or blocking the right lane or shoulder.

cards.front: Where must slow vehicles stay?
cards.back: Slow vehicles must stay in the right lane except to pass or turn left.

cards.front: Who may drive against the flow of traffic?
cards.back: Only emergency and police vehicles running lights and sirens may drive against the flow of traffic.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: On a freeway, when may you use the left lane?
cards.back: On an interstate or full-access controlled freeway you must keep right, using the left lane only when congestion or weather requires it or an obstacle or hazard sits in the right lane.

cards.front: What other reasons allow the freeway left lane?
cards.back: On those freeways you may also use the left lane to move over for emergency or construction vehicles, or when no traffic is right behind or ahead of you in that lane.

cards.front: Is weaving between lanes to speed through traffic allowed?
cards.back: Weaving between lanes to speed through traffic is illegal.

cards.front: May you drive across a median, and when may you use a cut-through?
cards.back: Driving across median strips or through barriers is illegal, but you may turn left through a paved median cut-through when no sign forbids it.

cards.front: Where may you enter and leave controlled-access roads?
cards.back: Enter and leave controlled-access roads only at designated, posted entrances and exits.

cards.front: How is a median cut-through different from crossing a median?
cards.back: A paved median cut-through with no prohibiting sign may be used for a left turn, while driving across median strips or through barriers is illegal.

cards.front: How is driving in an empty freeway left lane different from weaving?
cards.back: On a freeway, an empty left lane with no one right behind or ahead of you is a listed reason you may drive there, while weaving through traffic is never allowed.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: What steps make a safe right turn?
cards.back: For a right turn, use the correct lane and your signal, obey signs and signals, yield to pedestrians, emergency vehicles and other traffic, and check that your left side is clear.

cards.front: How do you steer through a right turn?
cards.back: During a right turn, follow the curve of the curb and stay out of other lanes.

cards.front: What do trucks and buses need when turning right?
cards.back: Trucks and buses need extra room to turn right.

cards.front: With multiple right-turn lanes, where do you finish the turn?
cards.back: With multiple right-turn lanes, finish the turn in the lane that matches the one you turned from, since drifting can cut off another driver and cause a crash.

cards.front: What steps make a safe left turn?
cards.back: For a left turn, use the correct lane and signal, obey signs and signals, and yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, emergency vehicles and other traffic.

cards.front: How should your front wheels point before a left turn begins?
cards.back: Keep your front wheels pointed straight until you actually begin a left turn.

cards.front: With multiple left-turn lanes, where do you end the turn?
cards.back: With multiple left-turn lanes, end the turn in the lane that corresponds to your turn lane.

cards.front: What should you look for before turning left?
cards.back: Check all approaching traffic before a left turn, looking for vehicles hidden behind or beside others, especially motorcycles, scooters and bicycles, which are easy to miss.

cards.front: Why stay in your matching lane in a double turn lane?
cards.back: In a double turn lane, staying in your matching lane prevents cutting off the driver turning beside you.

cards.front: What do you do with your wheels while waiting to turn left?
cards.back: While waiting to turn left, hold the front wheels straight ahead and turn them only as the turn begins.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: Must you signal turns, and who mostly uses hand signals now?
cards.back: Always signal turns; hand signals for left, right and stop are now used mostly by motorcyclists, scooter and moped riders and bicyclists.

cards.front: How do you move one lane to the left?
cards.back: To move left, check behind and to your left with a head check, signal left, and move over carefully.

cards.front: How do you move one lane to the right?
cards.back: To move right, check behind and to your right, signal right, and move over carefully.

cards.front: How do the head checks differ for moving left and moving right?
cards.back: A lane change to the left starts with a head check behind and to your left, while a change to the right checks behind and to your right.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: What is a roundabout, and whom do entering drivers yield to?
cards.back: A roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic moves counterclockwise around a central island and entering vehicles yield to traffic coming from the left, including bicyclists and pedestrians.

cards.front: How should you approach a roundabout?
cards.back: When approaching a roundabout, use signs and pavement markings to pick the right lane, slow down, stay right of the center island, and look left as you reach the yield line.

cards.front: How do you enter a roundabout, and what must you never do?
cards.back: Enter a roundabout when a suitable gap appears and merge with the flow, and never turn left to enter, which puts you in front of oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Whom should you watch for as you enter or exit a roundabout?
cards.back: Watch for pedestrians crossing as you enter or exit a roundabout.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: Who has the right of way inside a roundabout, and when do you stop?
cards.back: Inside a roundabout, stay right of the center island; vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you stop only when it is the only safe way to avoid a collision.

cards.front: How do you leave a roundabout?
cards.back: You leave a roundabout by turning right onto the road you want.

cards.front: An emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout. What do you do?
cards.back: If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, do not stop; leave at the nearest exit, pull right and stop to let it pass.

cards.front: When should you choose your roundabout lane?
cards.back: Choose your lane before entering a roundabout and avoid changing lanes inside it.

cards.front: How should you treat trucks and other vehicles in a roundabout?
cards.back: Avoid passing or driving beside trucks and trailers in a roundabout, as they may need more than one lane, and do not pass other vehicles, bicycles or mopeds.

cards.front: How do you exit a roundabout, and what if you miss your exit?
cards.back: When exiting, keep a slow speed, signal your exit, and wait to accelerate until you are past the exit's pedestrian crossing; if you miss your exit, go around again.

cards.front: Whom do you yield to entering a roundabout, and who yields to you inside?
cards.back: Entering a roundabout you yield to traffic from your left, but once inside you have the right of way over drivers waiting to enter.

cards.front: Do you stop in a roundabout for an emergency vehicle?
cards.back: In a roundabout you do not stop for an approaching emergency vehicle; you leave by the nearest exit and only then pull right and stop.

cards.front: How do you enter and exit a roundabout?
cards.back: You enter a roundabout by merging with the counterclockwise flow and exit by turning right, never by turning left.

cards.front: How do you fix a missed roundabout exit?
cards.back: Missing your roundabout exit is fixed by circling around again, not by stopping or changing lanes inside the circle.

decks.domain: Lane usage, turning, changing lanes and roundabouts

cards.front: What should you do at every railroad crossing, and why?
cards.back: Slow down and look both ways at every railroad crossing, because a train can need a mile or more to stop and is closer and faster than it looks.
cards.memory_hook: trains are closer than they look

cards.front: Where may people cross tracks, and what is illegal on them?
cards.back: Walkers, cyclists and drivers should cross tracks only at designated crossings, and walking along or stopping on tracks is illegal.

cards.front: What does the railroad advance warning sign mean, and where do you stop for a train?
cards.back: The railroad advance warning sign means a crossing is ahead; with a train coming, stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the tracks.

cards.front: How far do trains overhang the rails?
cards.back: Trains overhang the rails by at least three feet on each side, and cargo can stick out farther.

cards.front: Where do you stop for a train, and why does the near limit matter?
cards.back: At a railroad crossing with a train coming you stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the tracks, and the lower limit matters since trains overhang the rails by at least three feet.

recap_hooks.text: Keep right unless passing or avoiding an obstacle; road layouts, signs, emergencies and construction allow leaving it.
Slow vehicles keep right, and only lights and sirens drive against traffic.
On freeways keep right and use the left lane only for listed reasons; weaving is never allowed.
Use paved cut-throughs, never median strips, and only posted entrances and exits.
Turns start in the right lane with a signal and yielding; hug the curb right, keep wheels straight before a left.
In double turn lanes stay in your matching lane, and look for hidden motorcycles before turning left.
Always signal; look left before moving left and right before moving right.
Approach slowly in the right lane, yield to traffic from the left, and enter on a gap, never by turning left.
Watch for walkers at every roundabout crossing.
Inside, circulating traffic has the right of way; exit with a right turn, and go around again if you miss it.
For an emergency vehicle, exit first, then pull right and stop.
Slow and look at every crossing; with a train coming, stop between fifty and fifteen feet from the tracks.
Trains overhang the rails, so cross only at designated crossings.
